title: Agility Robotics' Nasdaq debut invites scrutiny of humanoid robot market
gist: Agility Robotics became the first US-listed dedicated humanoid robot company via a SPAC merger on Nasdaq on November 5, 2026, and its S-4 filing discloses unit economics: $8,500/month robots-as-a-service or $200,000 outright purchase, a $150,000 bill of materials falling to $30,000 at 10,000 units/year, and a $300 million order for 1,000 Digit 5 robots. The company had just $1.8 million revenue against a $140 million operating loss in 2025 and flags intensifying competition from Tesla, Boston Dynamics, Figure AI and others.

insights.claim: Agility Robotics listed on Nasdaq on November 5, 2026 via a merger with a special purpose acquisition company, becoming the first dedicated humanoid robot developer to be publicly traded in the US.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Gives public investors the first pure-play US humanoid robotics stock and a disclosed benchmark for private peers.
insights.locator: The robotics company, headquartered in Salem

insights.claim: Agility's own S-4 filing acknowledges that humanoid robots remain unproven at scale and have not achieved widespread commercialization, unlike industrial robots with decades of track record.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Management itself flags commercialization risk, a key caveat for valuing the humanoid category.
insights.locator: Humanoid robots remain unproven at scale

insights.claim: Agility leads competitors in commercial deployments, with Digit robots working at GXO warehouses, Schaeffler's South Carolina factory and Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada, and GXO is expanding from Georgia to North Carolina and Tennessee.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Repeat and expanding customer deployments are the strongest available evidence of real humanoid demand.
insights.locator: Agility is one of many startups

insights.claim: Besides Agility, China's Unitree is the other humanoid maker to open its books, having listed on the Shanghai STAR Market in August 2026, while most competitors remain private and undisclosed.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Two public comps now exist for benchmarking humanoid robot valuations across the US and China.
insights.locator: Another exception has been China’s humanoid

insights.claim: Under Agility's robots-as-a-service model customers pay about $25,000 per robot for deployment plus $8,500 per month, while the ownership model costs $200,000 for hardware, $20,000 for deployment and $36,000 per year for software and maintenance.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Establishes the first public price points for humanoid labor, enabling ROI comparisons against human wages.

insights.claim: CFO Michael Beer said a Digit subscription lets customers replace $200,000 in annual labor costs with $100,000 in robot costs, and outright purchase replaces $1.1 million in labor with about $400,000 in robot costs over five years.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: The pitch is roughly a 50-65% labor cost saving, the core driver of adoption if performance holds.
insights.locator: During a presentation for analysts and

insights.claim: Agility estimates each Digit 5 costs $150,000 in bill of materials today, falling to $75,000 at 1,000 units per year and $30,000 at 10,000 units per year, with a roughly five-year useful life.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Margins hinge on a 5x BOM cost-down through volume, making production ramp the critical variable.
insights.locator: The robotics company also estimated each

insights.claim: Agility pegs its own costs at $15,000 per robot per year for software and maintenance plus a one-time $15,000 deployment cost, and anticipates earning about $500,000 per robot under subscription and about $400,000 under ownership.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Implies high recurring gross margins on service, though the stated per-robot earnings figures warrant scrutiny against list prices.

insights.claim: Robots-as-a-service pricing is set near the human labor rate so customers see a return on day one, according to Agility co-founder Jonathan Hurst.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Labor-parity pricing lowers adoption friction and shifts hardware risk onto Agility's balance sheet.
insights.quote: they’re paying a rate that is comparable to the human labor rate, and that makes the economics pretty straightforward
insights.locator: When we are doing robots as

insights.claim: Agility's subscription revenue model is based on an unidentified customer's $300 million order for 1,000 Digit 5 robots over a three-year contract, contingent on meeting contractual milestones, features and specifications.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: A single large conditional order underpins the story, creating concentration and execution risk.

insights.claim: Agility generated just $1.8 million in revenue in 2025 against a $140 million operating loss and expects operating and net losses for the foreseeable future.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: The company is pre-commercial with heavy cash burn, so dilution and funding risk are central to the equity.
insights.quote: Agility has incurred net losses since inception and expects to continue to incur operating and net losses for the foreseeable future.
insights.locator: The robotics company’s financial disclosures also

insights.claim: Digit 5, shipping from 2027, lifts up to 50 pounds, works more than 20 hours per 24 using a custom battery pack from UK-based Nyobolt that delivers 90 minutes of runtime from a nine-minute charge, under an exclusive humanoid-robot agreement.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Near-continuous uptime is critical to labor-replacement ROI, and the Nyobolt exclusivity is a potential moat.
insights.locator: The fast-charging battery technology provided by

insights.claim: Digit 5 includes an onboard safety system that detects nearby humans and stands still or squats, which CTO Pras Velagapudi says could allow deployment beyond isolated work cells.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Safe human co-working would materially expand the addressable deployment environments.

insights.claim: Agility's filing warns competition is intensifying rapidly from well-funded entrants including Boston Dynamics, Tesla, Apptronik, Figure AI, 1X Technologies, Sanctuary AI, Hexagon and NEURA Robotics, many with greater brand and resources.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: First-mover advantage may erode quickly against better-capitalized rivals such as Tesla.

insights.claim: Hurst predicts that within a year multiple customers will share videos of Digit robots boringly doing work, and that the humanoid market will fragment into niches like the early auto industry rather than one winner.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Suggests a multi-winner market structure where niche specialization matters more than general capability.
insights.quote: some companies will build the Ford F-150 and some companies will build a Mazda Miata
insights.locator: It’ll look a bit like the

insights.claim: Hurst dismisses near-term deployment of humanoid robots in homes, saying no company's robot will walk into a living room to do dishes soon.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Tempers consumer humanoid hype; the near-term market is structured industrial and logistics work.
insights.quote: Digit 5 is not going to walk into your living room and do dishes and stuff like that
insights.locator: Although Hurst sees Agility’s path eventually
